subject: Service encapsulation & egress justification for Dedicated/Private environment

Subject: Quick Q: Why do outbound flows from Dedicated need NAT?

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks for the walkthrough last week. Our security team is looking at the network diagram you shared and has a question about outbound traffic from the Dedicated instance pool.

Specifically: why does Redwood require a centralized NAT gateway for egress rather than letting instances use ephemeral public IPs or direct cloud-provider-managed egress per-node? From our side, minimizing single points that carry customer traffic can help with availability and reduce blast radius.

Can you point me to the design rationale and any controls (logging, DLP, restricted destination lists) you use on that egress path? If you can attach a one-page justification and the updated diagram, that would help us close the SIG question.

Appreciate it — Julian

--
Julian Sanchez
Sr. Security Engineer, Maple Health
security@maplehealth.com
From: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwoodinference.com>
To: Julian Sanchez <j.sanchez@maplehealth.com>
Cc: Naomi Feldman <naomi.feldman@redwoodinference.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Thu, 15 Jul 2027 10:03:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Quick Q: Why do outbound flows from Dedicated need NAT?

Julian —

Good question. Short answer: we centralize egress for Dedicated/Private deployments to provide consistent control, observability, and policy enforcement across tenant pools. Long answer and attachments below.

Key reasons:
- Centralized policy enforcement: NAT egress sits behind our egress control plane so we can apply deny-lists, allow-lists, and IPS/IDS integrations in one place.
- Audit & provenance: all outbound flows are logged and tied to a customer-owned network tag; this makes SOC 2 evidence (flow logs + tamper-resistant export) straightforward.
- Cost and performance: for most workloads, a controlled pool reduces ephemeral IP churn and makes SNAT translation capacity predictable.
- Failover and controlled fallbacks: we have a multi-region egress mesh; if the primary NAT pool saturates, traffic can be routed to a warm standby region under policy.

Controls implemented on the egress path:
- Flow logging (retention per contract).
- TLS interception is NOT performed; we apply metadata-based allow/deny and destination categorization.
- DLP hooks via outbound URL categorization for regulated customers on Request.
- Integration with KMS for ephemeral outbound cert signing (when customers opt in).

I've attached: service-encapsulation-diagram.vsdx and a short egress-flow-table.csv mapping control objectives to artifacts. Also included a draft SIG answer summary.

If you want, we can run a short tabletop with your network team to walk the failover path.

Best,
Kimberly

--
Kimberly Park
Head of Product Security, Redwood Inference
From: Naomi Feldman <naomi.feldman@redwoodinference.com>

Date: Fri, 16 Jul 2027 08:25:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Quick Q: Why do outbound flows from Dedicated need NAT?

Julian — adding a few operational details that normally help auditors:

1) Tenant encapsulation: each customer’s compute nodes live in isolated subnets. Outbound is NAT’ed with a dedicated egress IP block mapped to the tenant tag. That mapping is recorded in our config DB and exported to customers as part of the audit bundle.

2) Logging & retention: Flow logs are exported to a customer-owned S3/GCS bucket when requested; by default we retain logs for 90 days. For SOC 2 engagements we can provide signed export manifests and checksums.

3) Deny-first posture: we maintain a default deny-list and allow-list by destination category; customers can request exceptions through the support portal.

4) No shared credentials: control plane actions that change NAT mapping require 2-person approval for Dedicated customers.

I'll open a short evidence ticket to attach the signed export examples and a traceroute test we ran in staging.

-naomi

- For the signed export manifest, do you include HMAC or other tamper-evidence? They prefer chained attestations.

If you can drop a short snippet to the thread and point to the diagram element that shows the tenant->egress mapping, we can mark the question resolved on our end.

Julian

- Manifest tamper-evidence: HMAC + SHA256 checksums, signed via HSM (key-id redwood-hsm-2027-07).
- Export artifacts: sample flow logs + traceroute PDF included in the ticket.
- Operational control: 2-person approval for NAT mapping changes; action logs exported to customer with the bundle.
